chapter_title: Motion in a Plane - River, Rain and Circular Motion
build_scope: Continue after Relative Motion through §7.3 Circular Motion; keep the supplied Formulae Sheet as a source cross-check.
core2_policy: Only link a learner concept to Revised Core (2) v2 when a matching challenge exists. Do not invent links for river, rain or circular-motion ideas that are absent from the 59-question revised set.

concepts.learner_title: Three arrows tell the boat's real motion
plain_language: A boat has one velocity through the water, while the water itself has another velocity relative to the ground.
The path seen from the river bank comes from adding those two velocity arrows.
model_notes: Use one x-y coordinate system for all three velocity vectors.
In the source setup, the stream flows along x and the river width is measured across y.

concepts.learner_title: Add the boat and stream arrows
plain_language: The boat-water arrow and stream arrow form a triangle or parallelogram. The diagonal is the motion seen from the bank.
Magnitude tells how fast the boat moves over the ground; direction tells where that resultant points.
model_notes: The angle symbols alpha and beta must match the source geometry before the formulas are used.

concepts.learner_title: Which part of the velocity gets you across?
plain_language: Only the across-river component closes the distance between the two banks.
The stream can push the boat sideways without helping it cover the river width.
model_notes: In the source geometry, theta is measured from the across-river direction.

concepts.learner_title: Fastest crossing is not the straightest path
plain_language: To cross in the least time, make the boat's across-river component as large as possible.
That usually means pointing directly across, but the stream then carries the boat downstream.
model_notes: The source minimum-time result uses theta = 0 in its across-river angle convention.

concepts.learner_title: Aim upstream to arrive directly opposite
plain_language: For zero drift, the boat must spend part of its speed fighting the stream upstream.
The upstream component cancels the stream; only the remaining across-river component carries the boat to the other bank.
model_notes: Zero drift is possible only when the boat's still-water speed is at least as large as the stream speed.

concepts.learner_title: Steer into the wind to travel straight
plain_language: Wind changes an aircraft's ground track in the same way a stream changes a boat's ground path.
The pilot chooses an air-velocity heading so that, after the wind is added, the ground resultant points toward the destination.
model_notes: The source Illustration 12 uses a closed velocity triangle and a required north-east resultant.

concepts.learner_title: A person walking inside a moving boat
plain_language: The person's motion relative to the ground is built in layers: person relative to boat, then boat relative to ground.
Solve the boat's ground motion first; then add the person's motion inside the boat.
model_notes: The source Illustration 13 is solved in two stages rather than by mixing all speeds at once.

concepts.learner_title: Why rain seems to tilt when you move
plain_language: Rain has one velocity relative to the ground, but a moving person sees the rain using a different frame.
Subtract the observer's velocity from the rain velocity; the direction of the result is the apparent direction of the rain.
model_notes: The source inverse-rain example uses two observations to reconstruct the hidden ground-frame rain components.

plain_language: Circular motion means following a circular path. The speed may stay constant or it may change.
The source uses a satellite, a stone on a rope and a car on a curved track as familiar examples.
model_notes: Angular displacement theta tells how far around the circle the object has turned.

concepts.learner_title: From turning rate to ordinary speed
plain_language: Angular velocity tells how quickly the angle changes. Angular acceleration tells how quickly angular velocity changes.
Radius turns angular rates into ordinary tangential speed and tangential acceleration.
model_notes: Use radians when connecting angular quantities directly to linear quantities such as v = r omega.

concepts.learner_title: Same speed, but the velocity keeps changing
plain_language: In uniform circular motion the speed can stay constant while the velocity changes because the direction keeps turning.
The velocity is tangent to the circle; the acceleration points inward toward the centre.
model_notes: Radial acceleration changes the direction of velocity, not its speed in uniform circular motion.

concepts.learner_title: Two accelerations with two different jobs
plain_language: When speed changes on a circular path, acceleration has two jobs at once.
The radial part turns the velocity inward; the tangential part changes how large the speed is.
model_notes: Radial and tangential accelerations are perpendicular, so their magnitudes combine with Pythagoras.
